source_evidence.quote:
This JMR paper contains five MTurk studies plus an additional study in which the authors analyzed scanner panel data. We chose to replicate Study 1 (N = 145) because it represented the simplest test of the authors’ hypothesis, and because its effect size was among the largest in the paper [
2
]. In this study, participants saw two brands of peanut butter, a premium brand and a store brand, along with their prices. The authors manipulated two factors. First, the left-digit price difference was either large ($4.00 vs. $2.99) or small ($4.01 vs. $3.00). Second, the peanut butters (and their prices) were either presented adjacently on the same screen, or one after the other on different screens. Participants evaluated the relative price of the store brand on a scale ranging from
very low
to
very high
. The researchers found that consumers showed a greater left-digit bias – evaluating the store brand to be relatively lower when it was $2.99 than when it was $3.00 – when the products and prices were presented on the same screen rather than sequentially.

source_evidence.quote: Students were compared on their school performance (standardized math and reading tests and grades), motivation (math ability self-concept, intrinsic motivation, vocational interests, and educational aspirations), parental educational expectations, students’ evaluation of school instruction (perceived quality and pressure), and subjective well-being. The gifted scored higher on math performance (rank-biserial r = .66/.81), math ability self-concept (.71), intrinsic motivation (.62), and investigative vocational interests (.65). Some smaller differences were found for realistic (.42) and social interests (–.37) and for pressure in math lessons (–.52). Results support Terman’s findings on gifted individuals’ psychological functioning and contradict negative stereotypes about the gifted.

source_evidence.quote:
At the core of our survey instrument is a priming experiment (Mutz 2011). Respon-
dents were randomly assigned to one of four different groups: a control group that
received no treatment; treatment group 1 received an inequality prime; treatment
group 2 received an immigration prime; treatment group 3 received a combina-
tion of both primes, with order randomized. Our primes consisted of a combina-
tion of different techniques applied by Magni (2021), and by Alesina, Miano and
Stantcheva (2023). The former uses a depiction of factual information with visual
stimuli; the latter use quizzing elements Alesina, Miano and Stantcheva (2023).
We propose that combining these maximizes the effect of our primes.

source_evidence.quote:
The immigration treatment was structured in the same way as the inequality



                                                                                  7
 treatment. First, we asked respondents to estimate the percentage of the German
immigrant population and from which two world regions most of the immigrants
originate. Subsequently, respondents are provided with (visual) information about
the size and growth of immigration in Germany. Lastly, a picture of a multicultural
workforce and a picture of asylum-seekers waiting at a train station are displayed.

source_evidence.section: dependent variables and differences from originals
source_evidence.quote:
As for redistribution preferences of respondents, we first recorded respondents’
agreement to increase the taxes for rich people as an indicator for their support of
redistribution, mirroring Alesina, Miano and Stantcheva (2023) and Magni (2021)
(see DV 2 in table 1 for further details). Then, to detect a possible divergence in

                                                                                                                        9
 support for redistribution, depending on whether the target are natives or immi-
grants, we included two items asking for respondents’ agreement with increasing
social welfare benefits, separately, once for natives and once for immigrants, fol-
lowing Magni (2021) (see DV 3 in table 1). This served as the base for our two
measures of welfare chauvinism in our analysis. We calculated the simple differ-
ence between the answers a respondent gave to these two items, resulting in a
scale from -6 to 6 with 0 indicating the support for welfare benefits for natives and
immigrants being the same, positive values indicating greater support for bene-
fits for natives exclusively, and negative values indicating the opposite. We then
combined these two items and the respondents’ support for redistribution to con-
struct a welfare chauvinism indicator identical to Magni (2021). Besides, while
Alesina, Miano and Stantcheva (2023) have several questions about immigrants’
access to welfare benefits, no question specifically reflects welfare chauvinism as
measured by Magni (2021) and us. The closest question is a rating question on
whether the government should focus on U.S.-born people or everyone, including
legal immigrants (DV 3 in table 1).

In our study, we can specifically test the effect of an immigration prime (with
facts and figures about immigration) on welfare chauvinism, expanding the analysis
of Alesina, Miano and Stantcheva (2023). Notably, the immigration prime relates
negatively to both measures of welfare chauvinism (see Models 4 and 5). Effects
are statistically significant (at the 5% level) and substantively relevant: In model

source_evidence.quote: A total of 412 toddlers ages 12-30 months who received ADOS-2 Toddler Module as well as a best estimate clinical (BEC) diagnosis, were included in this study. ADOS-2 Toddler Module cut-off scores were determined using the appropriate algorithms (Algorithm 1 for toddlers aged 12-20 months and those aged 21-30 months with <5 words, Algorithm 2 for toddlers aged 21-30 months with 5 words or more). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to assess cut-off scores that optimized sensitivity and specificity when compared against BEC diagnosis. The selected cut-off scores were examined using frequency tables to compare ADOS-2 classification against BEC diagnosis.
